title: MCP 2026 Specification: Stateless Core, Apps, and Tasks
content:
## Overview

A new Model Context Protocol (MCP) specification revision entered release candidate status as the **2026-07-28** release, with the final spec shipping on that date. It is the biggest revision to the protocol since MCP's November 2024 introduction (see `tool-use-and-agents` for the original architecture), and it delivers on a 2026 roadmap built around one central change: MCP's protocol core becomes **stateless**.

---

## Stateless Protocol Core

Prior MCP versions relied on a stateful session model, which pushed servers toward sticky sessions and made horizontal scaling awkward. The 2026-07-28 revision removes that requirement: the core protocol now scales on ordinary HTTP infrastructure — standard load balancers, auto-scaling groups, and stateless request routing — without requiring a client to stay pinned to one server instance. This is aimed squarely at enterprises running MCP servers at scale rather than as local stdio processes on a developer's machine.

---

## MCP Apps

**MCP Apps** lets a server ship an interactive HTML interface alongside its tools. Tools declare their UI templates ahead of time, so a host application (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or any other MCP client) can prefetch, cache, and security-review the UI before ever rendering it. When invoked, the interface renders inside a **sandboxed iframe** in the host — turning what used to be text-only tool results into small embedded apps (think: a rendered chart from a database-query tool, or a form from a ticketing tool) without the host needing bespoke code per server.

---

## Tasks Extension

The **Tasks extension** addresses long-running tool calls. Instead of a `tools/call` blocking until completion, a server can respond with a **task handle**. The client then drives the task forward with three new methods:

```
tasks/get      — poll current status
tasks/update   — receive progress/streaming updates
tasks/cancel   — cancel an in-flight task
```

Crucially, task creation is **server-directed** — the server decides whether a given call becomes a task, not the client — which keeps simple, fast tools on the existing synchronous path while giving slow operations (large crawls, batch jobs, multi-minute agent sub-tasks) a first-class async lifecycle instead of a client-side polling hack.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization

A companion extension, **Enterprise-Managed Authorization**, reached stable status alongside the spec RC. It enables organizations to centrally provision MCP server access through their existing identity provider, so a user gets access to approved connected servers on first login — no per-app OAuth consent screen required. This is a zero-touch OAuth model aimed at the same enterprise-rollout pain point the stateless core addresses: getting MCP deployed org-wide without a manual connection step per employee per server. Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta are named adopters, alongside a growing list of MCP servers.

---

## Ecosystem Adoption

MCP's governance has moved to the **Linux Foundation**, formalizing it as an open standard rather than an Anthropic-run project. By mid-2026, MCP support ships built into Claude Desktop, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Windsurf, and both OpenAI and Google have committed to MCP support in their own developer platforms — meaning the protocol Anthropic introduced in late 2024 is now a cross-vendor standard rather than a Claude-specific integration path. Test-automation platforms including Cypress, BrowserStack, and Maestro have also wired MCP servers into their actual product surfaces in 2026, extending the ecosystem beyond developer-tool and data-source integrations into QA tooling.

---

## Why This Matters

The 2024–2025 version of MCP proved the plug-and-play model for tool integration but was designed around a single long-lived client-server session — fine for a developer's local Claude Code instance, harder for a company running MCP servers behind a load balancer for thousands of users. The 2026-07-28 revision is squarely an enterprise-readiness release: stateless scaling, centrally managed auth, and a governance move to a neutral foundation all point toward MCP being treated as production infrastructure rather than a developer convenience.
